papers.conclusion: The study concludes that Chain-of-Thought prompting works by efficiently communicating task understanding and leveraging the model's ability to fill in commonsense knowledge, rather than by teaching step-by-step reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Specific symbols in the prompt do not significantly impact performance, but consistent patterns and web-style text are crucial.
The necessity of accurate few-shot examples depends on their role in communicating task understanding; inaccurate examples can sometimes improve performance.
Intermediate steps in COT primarily convey task understanding rather than teaching how to solve the task.
COT leverages LLMs to fill in missing commonsense information, aiding difficult reasoning and long-tail questions.
Patterns and symbols work together to generate missing information and reinforce task understanding.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a few tasks and models.
The definitions of symbols and patterns are task-specific and may not generalize.
Reliance on automatic metrics may not capture nuanced errors.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more tasks and models.
Incorporate human evaluation.
Explore generalization of symbols and patterns definitions.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of Chain-of-thought prompting (CoT) has been widely recognized, but the underlying mechanisms behind its success, the reason why it just works for a wide range of tasks, remains an open question. To investigate this, we employ a counterfactual prompting approach, systematically manipulating elements of examples used in a few-shot prompt, and testing the consequences on model behavior. This allows us to understand the relative contributions of prompt elements such as symbols (digits, entities) and patterns (equations, sentence structure) on in-context learning. Our experiments with three different large language models (LLMs) reveal several key findings. First, the specific symbols used in the prompt do not significantly impact the model’s performance. However, consistent patterns in examples and specifying text in style frequently found on the web are crucial. Second, our findings suggest that the necessity of accurate few-shot examples depends on their role in communicating task understanding. We identify tasks where inaccurate few-shot examples hurt and, surprisingly, tasks where they improve performance. Additionally, we find that the intermediate steps in CoT may not necessarily facilitate learning how to solve a task, but instead efficiently convey task understanding (what) to the model. Furthermore, CoT leverages LLMs to fill in missing commonsense information, particularly helping difficult reasoning problems and long-tail questions.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: CIP: A Plug-and-Play Causal Prompting Framework for Mitigating Hallucinations under Long-Context Noise
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) when processing long and noisy retrieval contexts be mitigated by using causal inference to steer reasoning toward causally relevant evidence?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CIP, a lightweight, plug-and-play prompting framework that restructures raw retrieval outputs into explicit causal relation chains to suppress non-causal reasoning paths, thereby mitigating hallucinations and improving factual grounding in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CIP effectively mitigates hallucinations in LLMs by infusing causal structures into the input representation, leading to more reliable, explainable, and efficient reasoning, highlighting causal reasoning as a promising paradigm for trustworthy AI.
papers.key_findings:
CIP consistently improves Attributable Rate (AR) and Causal Consistency Score (CCS) across seven mainstream LLMs, demonstrating enhanced factual reliability and logical coherence.
CIP's proactive causal analysis and parallel query dispatch reduce end-to-end response latency by up to 55.1% compared to reactive retrieval methods.
The framework improves effective information density in generated responses by filtering irrelevant content and preserving causally relevant evidence.
LoRA-based fine-tuning of the 7B-parameter CIP plugin efficiently corrects causal interpretation biases without updating the main LLM weights.
CIP's causal upstream intervention formally reduces robust hallucination risk under distribution shifts and improves generalization on long-document tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models often hallucinate when processing long and noisy retrieval contexts because they rely on spurious correlations rather than genuine causal relationships. We propose CIP, a lightweight and plug-and-play causal prompting framework that mitigates hallucinations at the input stage. CIP constructs a causal relation sequence among entities, actions, and events and injects it into the prompt to guide reasoning toward causally relevant evidence. Through causal intervention and counterfactual reasoning, CIP suppresses non causal reasoning paths, improving factual grounding and interpretability. Experiments across seven mainstream language models, including GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Llama 3.1, show that CIP consistently enhances reasoning quality and reliability, achieving 2.6 points improvement in Attributable Rate, 0.38 improvement in Causal Consistency Score, and a fourfold increase in effective information density. API level profiling further shows that CIP accelerates contextual understanding and reduces end to end response latency by up to 55.1 percent. These results suggest that causal reasoning may serve as a promising paradigm for improving the explainability, stability, and efficiency of large language models.

papers.title: DeCoT: Debiasing Chain-of-Thought for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks in Large Language Models via Causal Intervention
papers.research_question: How does internal knowledge bias in large language models impair chain-of-thought reasoning, and how can this bias be mitigated via causal intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal view to explain internal knowledge bias in LLMs and introduces DeCoT, a method that uses external knowledge as an instrumental variable and front-door adjustment to debias chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: DeCoT effectively alleviates the spurious correlation caused by internal knowledge bias, enabling LLMs to generate more accurate and logically sound chain-of-thought reasoning and final answers.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge bias in LLMs can trigger the use of irrelevant information in prompts, leading to incoherent reasoning chains that impair logical reasoning.
DeCoT, by estimating the average causal effect (ACE) of CoT paths and sampling CoTs with high ACE, effectively reduces spurious correlation and improves reasoning accuracy.
The method consistently improves performance across multiple knowledge-intensive tasks and LLM backbones compared to standard CoT and context-aware contrastive decoding baselines.
DeCoT is compatible with and can improve other reasoning frameworks like ReAct by incorporating counterfactual debiasing.
The number of selected entities and alternative entities for causal intervention impacts performance, with more entities generally leading to better results but at increased computational cost.
papers.limitation: As an inference-stage causal intervention method, the improvement is limited by the upper bound of the LLM's capacity.
future_direction: Incorporate unbiased causal learning methods in the model pretraining or instruction tuning stage for more robust CoT reasoning.
Study the theoretical causal foundation of CoT prompting's mediator role in LLMs for better interpretability.
papers.abstract: Junda Wu, Tong Yu, Xiang Chen, Haoliang Wang, Ryan Rossi, Sungchul Kim, Anup Rao, Julian McAuley. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: In Machina N400: Pinpointing Where a Causal Language Model Detects Semantic Violations
papers.research_question: At which computational depth does a transformer first register a semantic anomaly, and does this temporal pattern align with the timing of the human N400 response?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that semantic anomaly detection in the transformer model Phi-2 emerges in mid-to-late layers, with decoding accuracy peaking around layer 22, and reveals a biphasic representational geometry with initial expansion followed by compression, paralleling human N400 dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that both artificial and biological language systems may postpone semantic anomaly detection until sufficient context is integrated, with parallels to human N400 responses, though mechanisms may differ.
papers.key_findings:
Decoding accuracy for semantic violations peaks at layer 22 with AUC 0.723, and is significant only in layers 18-30.
Participation ratio analysis shows that violations initially increase dimensionality in early layers (1-6), then decrease below control levels after layer 12.
The late emergence of anomaly detection suggests semantic integration occurs after syntactic processing, similar to human language comprehension.
papers.limitation:
Results are from a single model (Phi-2) and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
Stimuli have fixed violation position, which could allow the model to exploit positional regularity.
Only participation ratio was used for geometry analysis; other measures might reveal additional structure.
Statistical robustness relies on five-fold cross-validation; larger corpora could improve generality.
Linear logistic regression was the primary probe; non-linear methods might provide further insights.
future_direction: Replicate analysis in larger autoregressive LMs and bidirectional encoders to test architecture generality.
Randomize violation position and introduce graded expectancy manipulations in stimuli.
Use complementary geometry metrics like intrinsic dimensionality or manifold capacity.
papers.abstract: How and where does a transformer notice that a sentence has gone semantically off the rails? To explore this question, we evaluated the causal language model (phi-2) using a carefully curated corpus, with sentences that concluded plausibly or implausibly. Our analysis focused on the hidden states sampled at each model layer. To investigate how violations are encoded, we utilized two complementary probes. First, we conducted a per-layer detection using a linear probe. Our findings revealed that a simple linear decoder struggled to distinguish between plausible and implausible endings in the lowest third of the model's layers. However, its accuracy sharply increased in the middle blocks, reaching a peak just before the top layers. Second, we examined the effective dimensionality of the encoded violation. Initially, the violation widens the representational subspace, followed by a collapse after a mid-stack bottleneck. This might indicate an exploratory phase that transitions into rapid consolidation. Taken together, these results contemplate the idea of alignment with classical psycholinguistic findings in human reading, where semantic anomalies are detected only after syntactic resolution, occurring later in the online processing sequence.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning. Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Missed Causes and Ambiguous Effects: Counterfactuals Pose Challenges for Interpreting Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What problems arise from using counterfactual theories of causality in neural network interpretability, specifically regarding overdetermination and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two key challenges in using counterfactual interventions for interpretability: overdetermination (redundant causes are missed) and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies, which bias findings and complicate causal graph extraction.
papers.conclusion: Counterfactual theories of causality are sufficient for interpreting neural networks, but researchers must account for their pitfalls—non-transitivity and overdetermination—by using diverse data, multiple intervention types, and careful interpretation of causal graphs.
papers.key_findings:
Counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, complicating the interpretation of causal chains.
Overdetermination (multiple sufficient causes) leads counterfactual methods to systematically miss certain causes, lowering recall.
Local causal dependencies (nodes that affect intermediate components but not the output directly) should be included in circuits to understand how abstractions are composed.
Using diverse datasets and both positive and negative counterfactuals can help mitigate these issues.
Counterfactual theories are still the most actionable for interpretability, but must be applied with awareness of their limitations.
future_direction: Use more diverse datasets and held-out evaluation sets to improve generalization of interpretability methods.
Employ both positive and negative counterfactuals (ablating and injecting activations) to capture redundant causes.
Create toy models with built-in overdetermination and preemption to develop and test methods that handle these challenges.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research takes counterfactual theories of causality for granted. Most causal methods rely on counterfactual interventions to inputs or the activations of particular model components, followed by observations of the change in models' output logits or behaviors. While this yields more faithful evidence than correlational methods, counterfactuals nonetheless have key problems that bias our findings in specific and predictable ways. Specifically, (i) counterfactual theories do not effectively capture multiple independently sufficient causes of the same effect, which leads us to miss certain causes entirely; and (ii) counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, which complicates methods for extracting and interpreting causal graphs from neural networks. We discuss the implications of these challenges for interpretability researchers and propose concrete suggestions for future work.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models perform multi-step reasoning? The paper aims to uncover the reasoning mechanisms (thought processes) used by language models in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF), which combines circuit analysis and self-influence functions to trace and analyze the reasoning pathways of language models, demonstrating its application on GPT-2 for the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that SICAF successfully maps reasoning pathways in language models, revealing a hierarchical reasoning structure similar to human thought processes.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace the thought process of language models during complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified by EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL are more faithful and compact than those identified by EAP.
The model's key parameters are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The reasoning process follows a hierarchical structure: early layers identify entities, middle layers interpret actions, and final layers synthesize information.
Self-influence scores show how token importance changes across layers, revealing the reasoning path.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
Our work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of this approach across varied tasks and model architectures
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success; however, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque due to the complexity of non-linear interactions and high-dimensional operations. While previous studies have demonstrated that these models implicitly embed reasoning trees, humans typically employ various distinct logical reasoning mechanisms to complete the same task. It is still unclear which multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve such tasks. In this paper, we aim to address this question by investigating the mechanistic interpretability of language models, particularly in the context of multi-step reasoning tasks. Specifically, we employ circuit analysis and self-influence functions to evaluate the changing importance of each token throughout the reasoning process, allowing us to map the reasoning paths adopted by the model. We apply this methodology to the GPT-2 model on a prediction task (IOI) and demonstrate that the underlying circuits reveal a human-interpretable reasoning process used by the model.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Causal Consistency Regularization: Training Verifiably Sensitive Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we train large language models to be more faithful in their reasoning by making their answers sensitive to logical perturbations in the reasoning trace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Counterfactual Sensitivity Regularization (CSR), a training paradigm that improves reasoning faithfulness by enforcing causal consistency between reasoning traces and outputs through operator-level interventions and KL divergence regularization.
papers.conclusion: CSR is an effective training paradigm for verifiable reasoning in structured domains, substantially improving faithfulness with strong generalization and efficiency, establishing a new Pareto frontier.
papers.key_findings:
CSR improves Counterfactual Outcome Sensitivity (COS) by 25-35 points on benchmarks like GSM8K, HotpotQA, ProofWriter, and PubMedQA.
CSR generalizes to held-out perturbation types and cross-domain transfer, indicating it learns general faithfulness principles.
CSR achieves a new Pareto frontier in efficiency-faithfulness trade-off, with only ~9% training overhead.
CSR models show improved human and LLM-judged faithfulness ratings, with 4.1/5 human rating vs 2.3 for standard fine-tuning.
CSR prevents spurious shortcut reliance and routes computation through reasoning traces, as shown by causal tracing with 3.4× higher indirect effect.
papers.limitation:
CSR is most effective in structured reasoning domains where operators are unambiguously identifiable; in open-ended domains, operator identification precision drops, yielding limited improvements.
CSR requires a verifier capable of identifying when counterfactual edits break logical validity; optimal performance requires precision above 78%.
future_direction: Develop universal meta-verifiers for unseen domains.
Explore causal discovery methods for automatic operator identification.
Create semantic guardrails for open-ended reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce correct answers while relying on flawed reasoning traces, partly because common training objectives reward final-answer correctness rather than faithful intermediate reasoning. This undermines trustworthiness in high-stakes settings. We propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Regularization (CSR), a training paradigm that improves reasoning faithfulness by enforcing causal consistency between reasoning steps and outcomes. CSR automatically applies operator-level interventions to reasoning traces, such as swapping "+" with "-", to generate minimally perturbed counterfactual rationales, and penalizes the model when these logically invalid traces still lead to the original answer. Our implementation is efficient, adding about 9 percent training overhead via a warm-start curriculum and token-subset optimization. We evaluate faithfulness using Counterfactual Outcome Sensitivity (COS), which measures how appropriately answers change under logical perturbations. Across arithmetic (GSM8K), logical deduction (ProofWriter), multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), and code generation (MBPP), CSR yields improved accuracy versus faithfulness trade-offs, establishing a new Pareto frontier. CSR improves faithfulness over standard fine-tuning and process supervision by up to 70 percentage points, and transfers across model families with 94.2 to 96.7 percent success in structured domains. CSR also complements inference-time methods such as self-consistency. Overall, CSR offers a practical route to more reliable reasoning in structured domains, including mathematics, formal logic, and code, where operators are well-defined and verifiable, covering an estimated 40 to 60 percent of high-stakes reasoning deployments.

papers.title: Localizing Model Behavior with Path Patching
papers.research_question: How can we localize behaviors of neural networks to a subset of components or interactions, and how can we quantitatively test hypotheses about such localization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing hypotheses that model behaviors are localized to specific sets of paths in a computational graph.
papers.conclusion: Path patching is an expressive formalism for localization claims that is both principled and sufficiently efficient to run on real models.
papers.key_findings:
The minimal explanation of induction heads is insufficient; a refined hypothesis including additional paths (e.g., from layer 0 heads to induction heads) explains more of the behavior.
Path patching can produce sparser and more precise localizations than causal tracing or zero ablation.
Head 1.5 in the studied model implements both induction and a distinct 'parroting' heuristic for repeating tokens.
Path patching attribution can identify specific inputs where a hypothesis is unfaithful, guiding iterative refinement.
papers.limitation:
Measures sufficiency rather than completeness; a set of paths with low AUE may not be the complete set of paths responsible for the behavior.
Provides no evidence about downstream tasks; low AUE does not guarantee the abstraction is useful for applications.
Makes no claims outside the tested distribution; low AUE on one dataset does not imply low AUE on a wider distribution.
Cannot reject all false hypotheses due to potential cancellation effects in metrics like difference in expected loss.
Cannot definitively prove hypotheses, as testing all possible inputs is infeasible.
Demonstrations are narrow in scope compared to the full range of behaviors exhibited by language models.
future_direction: Scaling path patching to state-of-the-art models.
Using interpretability to detect distribution shift.
Producing adversarial examples based on knowledge of model mechanisms.
Automating hypothesis search over combinations of paths.
papers.abstract: Localizing behaviors of neural networks to a subset of the network's components or a subset of interactions between components is a natural first step towards analyzing network mechanisms and possible failure modes. Existing work is often qualitative and ad-hoc, and there is no consensus on the appropriate way to evaluate localization claims. We introduce path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing a natural class of hypotheses expressing that behaviors are localized to a set of paths. We refine an explanation of induction heads, characterize a behavior of GPT-2, and open source a framework for efficiently running similar experiments.

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance. Unlike prior approaches in mechanistic interpretability, which are hypothesis-driven and require prompt templates or target labels, CHG applies directly to any dataset using standard next-token prediction. We evaluate CHG across multiple large language models (LLMs) in the Llama 3 model family and diverse tasks, including syntax, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning, and show that CHG scores yield causal, not merely correlational, insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analyses. We also introduce contrastive CHG, a variant that isolates sub-circuits for specific task components. Our findings reveal that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, that individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity), and that instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.

papers.title: Editing Common Sense in Transformers
papers.research_question: Whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and if so, can model editing effectively repair incorrect commonsense plausibility judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates strong causal relations between commonsense plausibility judgments and early MLP layers in Transformers, and introduces MEMIT_CSK, an improved model editing method for commonsense that outperforms fine-tuning baselines.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that commonsense knowledge is localized in early MLP layers and can be effectively edited with MEMIT_CSK, providing a compelling direction for incorporating commonsense feedback into transformers through direct model editing.
papers.key_findings:
High task performance is crucial for achieving strong causal tracing results.
Targeted part of speech and layer locations affect causal tracing conclusions and edit success.
MEMIT_CSK exhibits configuration generalization (hyperparameters transfer well to unseen data).
MEMIT_CSK exhibits semantic generalization (balances affected and unaffected neighborhoods).
MEMIT_CSK outperforms fine-tuning for repairing commonsense knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Unable to investigate larger open-sourced models like GPT-J and GPT-NeoX due to resource limitations.
Focus on the binary plausibility prediction task, while parameter editing could improve models on various commonsense tasks.
The optimal edit token (subject, verb, or object) varies among datasets; a single generalized optimal edit token requires further investigation.
future_direction: Investigating the research questions on larger models.
Extending parameter editing to improve models on various commonsense tasks.
Further investigation into the existence of a single generalized optimal edit token.
papers.abstract: Editing model parameters directly in Transformers makes updating open-source transformer-based models possible without re-training (Meng et al., 2023). However, these editing methods have only been evaluated on statements about encyclopedic knowledge with a single correct answer. Commonsense knowledge with multiple correct answers, e.g., an apple can be green or red but not transparent, has not been studied but is as essential for enhancing transformers' reliability and usefulness. In this paper, we investigate whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and we provide an affirmative answer. We find that directly applying the MEMIT editing algorithm results in sub-par performance and improve it for the commonsense domain by varying edit tokens and improving the layer selection strategy, i.e., $MEMIT_{CSK}$. GPT-2 Large and XL models edited using $MEMIT_{CSK}$ outperform best-fine-tuned baselines by 10.97% and 10.73% F1 scores on PEP3k and 20Q datasets. In addition, we propose a novel evaluation dataset, PROBE SET, that contains unaffected and affected neighborhoods, affected paraphrases, and affected reasoning challenges. $MEMIT_{CSK}$ performs well across the metrics while fine-tuning baselines show significant trade-offs between unaffected and affected metrics. These results suggest a compelling future direction for incorporating feedback about common sense into Transformers through direct model editing.

papers.title: Reducing Bias in Sentiment Analysis Models Through Causal Mediation Analysis and Targeted Counterfactual Training
papers.research_question: How to reduce bias in sentiment analysis models by leveraging causal mediation analysis to identify biased components and applying targeted counterfactual training for de-biasing.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a bias reduction method for sentiment analysis models that uses causal mediation analysis to identify layers causally implicated in gender bias and then applies counterfactual training only to those targeted layers, achieving improved fairness without loss of accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reduces gender bias in BERT sentiment models by using causal mediation analysis to target specific layers and then applying counterfactual training, resulting in improved fairness without compromising accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Causal mediation analysis can identify specific layers in BERT that contribute to gender bias.
Targeted counterfactual training on those identified layers reduces bias effectively.
The proposed method achieves higher fairness (lower Wasserstein distance) compared to baseline methods like full-model counterfactual training and dropout regularization.
The method maintains sentiment prediction accuracy while improving fairness, avoiding the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
The approach is validated on two sentiment analysis datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and evaluated on the Equity Evaluation Corpus (EEC).
papers.limitation: Limited to two datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and one fairness metric (p-Wasserstein).
future_direction: Apply the method to other biases on sensitive attributes such as ethnic groups, skin colour, and country.
Test the method on a broader range of datasets and with more fairness evaluation techniques.
Quantify the accuracy-fairness trade-off in real-world datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models provide high-accuracy solutions in many natural language processing tasks. In particular, they are used as word embeddings in sentiment analysis models. However, these models pick up on and amplify biases and social stereotypes in the data. Causality theory has recently driven the development of effective algorithms to evaluate and mitigate these biases. Causal mediation was used to detect biases, while counterfactual training was proposed to mitigate bias. In both cases, counterfactual sentences are created by changing an attribute, such as the gender of a noun, for which no change in the model output is expected. Biases are detected and eventually corrected each time the model behaviour differs between the original and the counterfactual sentence. We propose a new method for de-biasing sentiment analysis models that leverages the causal mediation analysis to identify the parts of the model primarily responsible for the bias and apply targeted counterfactual training for model de-biasing. We validated the methodology by fine-tuning the pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment prediction. We trained two sentiment analysis models using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset and the Amazon Product Reviews, respectively, and we evaluated the fairness and prediction performances using the Equity Evaluation Corpus. We illustrated the causal patterns in the network and showed that our method achieves both high fairness and more accurate sentiment analysis than the state-of-the-art approach. Contrary to state-of-the-art models, we achieved a noticeable improvement in gender fairness without hindering sentiment prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Gumbel Counterfactual Generation From Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we generate true string counterfactuals from language models by reformulating them as structural equation models using the Gumbel-max trick?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for generating true string counterfactuals from language models by reformulating them as structural equation models using the Gumbel-max trick, and develops an algorithm based on hindsight Gumbel sampling to infer latent noise variables and generate counterfactuals.
papers.conclusion: The Gumbel counterfactual generation framework provides a rigorous method for counterfactual analysis in language models and reveals that common intervention techniques are not surgical and induce unintended changes.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Gumbel counterfactual generation method produces meaningful counterfactual strings.
Common intervention techniques (e.g., MEMIT, linear steering, instruction tuning) have considerable undesired side effects, as evidenced by the edit distance between original and counterfactual sentences.
Even localized parameter modifications intended to change specific features can have broader, unintended impacts on model behavior.
future_direction: Exploring other choices beyond Gumbel noise for modeling the causal process.
papers.abstract: Understanding and manipulating the causal generation mechanisms in language models is essential for controlling their behavior. Previous work has primarily relied on techniques such as representation surgery -- e.g., model ablations or manipulation of linear subspaces tied to specific concepts -- to \emph{intervene} on these models. To understand the impact of interventions precisely, it is useful to examine \emph{counterfactuals} -- e.g., how a given sentence would have appeared had it been generated by the model following a specific intervention. We highlight that counterfactual reasoning is conceptually distinct from interventions, as articulated in Pearl's causal hierarchy. Based on this observation, we propose a framework for generating true string counterfactuals by reformulating language models as a structural equation model using the Gumbel-max trick, which we called Gumbel counterfactual generation. This reformulation allows us to model the joint distribution over original strings and their counterfactuals resulting from the same instantiation of the sampling noise. We develop an algorithm based on hindsight Gumbel sampling that allows us to infer the latent noise variables and generate counterfactuals of observed strings. Our experiments demonstrate that the approach produces meaningful counterfactuals while at the same time showing that commonly used intervention techniques have considerable undesired side effects.

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: Contextualize-then-Aggregate: Circuits for In-Context Learning in Gemma-2 2B
papers.research_question: What mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a few-shot prompt during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a two-step 'contextualize-then-aggregate' circuit for in-context learning in Gemma-2, where lower layers contextualize individual few-shot examples and higher layers aggregate this information to predict the next token.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a two-stage procedure for in-context learning where the model contextualizes representations of individual few-shot examples before aggregating them to prepare the next-token prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a two-step strategy: contextualization of individual few-shot examples in lower layers, followed by aggregation of task information in higher layers.
The aggregation step alone is insufficient for full performance on some tasks; contextualization is crucial, especially with ambiguous examples.
The identified circuits recover at least 90% of the full model's performance across five ICL tasks.
The information transported differs by edge type: aggregation edges generally move task information, while contextualization edges move information about input/output spaces.
The importance and specific edges of the contextualization subcircuit vary between tasks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to five tasks and one model family (Gemma-2).
Circuit discovery relies on patching, which requires careful design of counterfactual inputs.
The study does not provide a full interpretation of all individual components in the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more tasks and models.
Investigate the role of contextualization in other settings, such as linear regression tasks.
Provide a more fine-grained interpretation of individual components.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is an intriguing ability of large language models (LLMs). Despite a substantial amount of work on its behavioral aspects and how it emerges in miniature setups, it remains unclear which mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a fewshot prompt. We use causal interventions to identify information flow in Gemma-2 2B for five naturalistic ICL tasks. We find that the model infers task information using a two-step strategy we call contextualize-then-aggregate: In the lower layers, the model builds up representations of individual fewshot examples, which are contextualized by preceding examples through connections between fewshot input and output tokens across the sequence. In the higher layers, these representations are aggregated to identify the task and prepare prediction of the next output. The importance of the contextualization step differs between tasks, and it may become more important in the presence of ambiguous examples. Overall, by providing rigorous causal analysis, our results shed light on the mechanisms through which ICL happens in language models.

papers.title: Counterfactual Divergence Singularity: A Theoretical Model of High-Similarity Instability and Micro-Counterfactual Drift in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the relationship between input similarity and output divergence in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations be formalized, and what explains the instability near high similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS), a theoretical framework that characterizes instability in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations, showing that divergence increases sharply as semantic similarity approaches unity.
papers.conclusion: The Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS) captures instability in LLMs under micro-counterfactual perturbations, reframing challenges like hallucination as manifestations of local non-smoothness in semantic manifolds, and suggests new evaluation paradigms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Divergence exhibits a hyperbolic blow-up as semantic similarity approaches 1.
Semantic curvature increases logarithmically in high-similarity regimes.
Embedding drift is minimal for high-similarity pairs, but divergence is high, indicating a contradiction.
LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth, leading to instability near the identity boundary.
The CDS phenomenon provides a geometric explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Scale and computational constraints with only 200 micro-counterfactual pairs.
Dependency on a single paraphraser (FLAN-T5-Base).
Dependence on a single embedding model (SBERT MiniLM-L6-v2).
Absence of output-level probability divergence analysis.
Limited to English-language textual inputs.
Interpretational boundaries, not claiming CDS explains all hallucinations.
future_direction: Scaling to larger datasets (e.g., 2,000–20,000 pairs).
Testing with different paraphrasers and embedding models.
Including output-level probability divergence analysis.
Extending to other languages and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable fluency and contextual sensitivity, yet their behaviour under minimal semantic perturbations remains poorly understood. In particular, near-identical paraphrastic inputs—expected to yield stable and equivalent responses—often produce disproportionately divergent generative behaviour. This paper introduces the <bold>Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS)</bold> , a theoretical and empirical framework that characterizes a previously underexplored instability regime in transformer-based language models. This work formalizes micro-counterfactual perturbations as infinitesimal semantic variations in embedding space and show that, as semantic similarity approaches unity, divergence metrics exhibit a hyperbolic blow-up. Using a controlled experimental pipeline based on FLAN-T5-generated paraphrases and Sentence-BERT semantic embeddings, this paper empirically demonstrate that divergence, curvature, and embedding drift collectively reveal a singular boundary where semantic proximity no longer guarantees behavioural stability. Despite minimal embedding displacement and near-maximal cosine similarity, reciprocal divergence measures increase sharply, exposing a structural nonlinearity in the input–output mapping of LLMs. The results suggest that LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth and that standard embedding-based similarity metrics fail to capture instability near the identity boundary. This phenomenon provides a geometric and mathematical explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and certain forms of hallucination observed in generative systems. By reframing these behaviours as consequences of latent-space singularities rather than isolated decoding artifacts, this work contributes a novel theoretical lens for evaluating robustness, interpretability, and reliability in large language models.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models generalize to implications of facts they are finetuned on, and what mechanisms (extractive structures) enable this out-of-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the extractive structures framework to explain how language models generalize to implications of finetuned facts, and empirically validates two predictions of how these structures are learned: a data ordering effect and a weight grafting effect.
papers.conclusion: The extractive structures framework provides a mechanism for understanding out-of-context reasoning, and the empirical findings (data ordering and weight grafting) support the hypothesis that these structures are learned during pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extractive structures (informative, upstream, downstream components) are identified in the OLMo-7b model for two-hop reasoning tasks, with MLPs and attention heads playing specific roles.
Fact learning occurs in both early and late layers, with early layers enabling first-hop generalization and late layers enabling second-hop generalization.
A data ordering effect is observed: extractive structures are learned only if facts precede their implications during training.
Weight grafting (weight-space arithmetic) can transfer newly learned extractive structures to predict counterfactual implications.
Attention heads, not just MLPs, can store factual information as weight changes.
papers.limitation: The nature of an alternative mechanism hinted at in the data ordering experiments remains unclear, and the finetuning process's dependence on hyperparameters and the pretrained model is not fully characterized.
future_direction: Developing an underlying theory of generalization that captures the dynamical nature of optimization.
Applying the extractive structures framework more broadly to understand and ground out-of-context generalization beyond two-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) can generalize to implications of facts that they are finetuned on. For example, if finetuned on ``John Doe lives in Tokyo," LMs can correctly answer ``What language do the people in John Doe's city speak?'' with ``Japanese''. However, little is known about the mechanisms that enable this generalization or how they are learned during pretraining. We introduce extractive structures as a framework for describing how components in LMs (e.g., MLPs or attention heads) coordinate to enable this generalization. The structures consist of informative components that store training facts as weight changes, and upstream and downstream extractive components that query and process the stored information to produce the correct implication. We hypothesize that extractive structures are learned during pretraining when encountering implications of previously known facts. This yields two predictions: a data ordering effect where extractive structures can be learned only if facts precede their implications, and a weight grafting effect where extractive structures can be transferred to predict counterfactual implications. We empirically demonstrate these phenomena in the OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b, and Qwen 2-7b models. Of independent interest, our results also indicate that fact learning can occur at both early and late layers, which lead to different forms of generalization.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Learn Independent Causal Mechanisms?
papers.research_question: Can Large Language Models learn Independent Causal Mechanisms, and can a modular architecture with causal constraints improve out-of-distribution performance on abstract and causal reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new modular LLM architecture (ICLM) that integrates Independent Causal Mechanism principles, showing it can improve out-of-distribution performance on abstract and causal reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a modular architecture that enables LLMs to behave as Independent Causal Mechanisms, theoretically and experimentally showing improved reasoning and generalization, though modules remain partially dependent on shared domain-invariant knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ICLM architecture improves out-of-distribution performance on abstract and causal reasoning tasks compared to baseline models.
The modules specialize to their domain but still partially rely on a shared domain-invariant mechanism, indicating a limitation in representing fully independent mechanisms.
The routing strategy effectively separates inputs by format (text vs. symbolic) and sometimes by distribution, influencing performance.
Mutual information minimization reduces dependence between modules but does not eliminate it entirely, as modules remain correlated at inference.
The architecture shows promise in continual learning settings, mitigating catastrophic forgetting to some extent.
papers.limitation:
The model is constrained to a modular architecture with a single connection at the language modelling head, limiting expressivity for complex causal graphs.
The work does not attempt to directly represent the true causal mechanisms of the tasks, as they are unknown.
Experiments focus on reasoning tasks to study modularity and generalization, not on outperforming state-of-the-art.
High computational cost of training LLMs limited the experiments to a single fine-tuning run per task.
papers.abstract: Despite impressive performance on language modelling and complex reasoning tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) fall short on the same tasks in uncommon settings or with distribution shifts, exhibiting a lack of generalisation ability. By contrast, systems such as causal models, that learn abstract variables and causal relationships, can demonstrate increased robustness against changes in the distribution. One reason for this success is the existence and use of Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICMs) representing high-level concepts that only sparsely interact. In this work, we apply two concepts from causality to learn ICMs within LLMs. We develop a new LLM architecture composed of multiple sparsely interacting language modelling modules. We show that such causal constraints can improve out-of-distribution performance on abstract and causal reasoning tasks. We also investigate the level of independence and domain specialisation and show that LLMs rely on pre-trained partially domain-invariant mechanisms resilient to fine-tuning.

papers.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
papers.research_question: Can MLP neurons serve as a sparse basis for circuit tracing, comparable to sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs for circuit tracing, enabling effective circuit tracing without additional training costs.
papers.conclusion: MLP neurons provide a sparse basis for circuit tracing, advancing automated interpretability without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations are a much sparser basis than MLP outputs for circuit tracing, reducing circuit size by 100x.
Using RelP attribution closes the performance gap between MLP activations and SAE features.
The findings hold even with unpaired data (without counterfactual inputs).
RelP finds more faithful edges than Integrated Gradients for circuit tracing.
